description: We'll be creating a 2d simulator game for junior astronauts in a style similar to 60 seconds
summary:
This project is a proof of concept about a possible solution regarding the amount of time people spend on their devices. On average, teenagers spend 8 hours a day on their phones, which means that for a life expectancy of 75 years, we'd spend 25 years on our screens. Of those 25 years, how much is really used for something significant, and how much is just wasted, scrolling or playing useless videogames?

Our project is a proof of concept of a videogame, whose development is targeted towards being addictive, yet pedagogic, and educative. A game that allows its players to develop critical thinking and problem solving skills.

The game is set on mars, where you play as a group of astronauts who have been abandoned in its surface. Your goal is to manage a shelter and its resources, critically deciding which supplies are more important than others, at any given time.
details:
Our project consists of a role-playing survival game in which the player takes on the role of a member of an astronaut crew stranded on Mars. The objective is to survive as long as possible, managing resources and dealing with unexpected situations, until the rescue arrives.

We believe that younger generations are spending a lot of time with digital entertainment. In the United States, children aged 8 to 12 spend an average of approximately five hours per day using their phones (Common Sense Media, 2026). We saw an opportunity to turn some of that screen time into a meaningful experience where they can be introducced into aerospace technologies and increase their critical thinking.

One of our main design principles was to make the experience accessible without oversimplifying it or overwhelm with to many indicators, or complicated mechanics. The point was to find a balance between educational value and entertainment.

The project was developed using the resources available to both team members. We used personal computers for development, C as the programming language, LaTeX for the game document, PowerPoint for the presentation, and Inkscape for editing the visual elements.

We believe that the project's greatest creative value lies in its potential to positively influence young students by bringing them closer to STEM.

Throughout the project, we had to consider several factors, particularly time, available resources, technical capabilities, and creativity.

We consider this project is a starting point for further improvement, for example, expanding its mechanics and improving visual presentation.
